evidence.evidence_gap: Direct retrieval from the immediately previous lesson.

hints: Use the fixed product f lambda.
walkthrough: Every electromagnetic wave has speed c in free space.
The numerical value is $3.00\times10^8$ m s$^{-1}$.
With c fixed, increasing frequency requires wavelength to decrease.

ai_rubric.observable: States the free-space speed as $3.00\times10^8$ m s$^{-1}$ or c.
States that wavelength decreases when frequency increases.

hints: Write the long-to-short spectrum order before checking each option.
walkthrough: The local long-to-short order is infrared, visible, ultraviolet.
Infrared has the largest wavelength of these three and ultraviolet the smallest.
Select option B.

evidence.evidence_gap: No primary P2 leaf exists for the visible-range outcome.

hints: Recall the visible interval in nanometres.
walkthrough: Visible wavelengths are approximately 400 to 700 nm.
Only 500 nm lies in this interval.
Select option B.

hints: Compare the wavelength with the approximate $10^{-11}$ m to $10^{-8}$ m band.
walkthrough: This is the approximate X-ray range.
Select option C.

hints: Recite the section from microwave to ultraviolet.
walkthrough: From longer to shorter wavelength the local order is microwave, infrared, visible, ultraviolet.
The two gaps are infrared and visible light.

ai_rubric.observable: Places visible light after infrared and before ultraviolet.

hints: Use 1 nm = $10^{-9}$ m for both endpoints.
walkthrough: The approximate visible range is 400 to 700 nm.
Multiply each endpoint by $10^{-9}$ m per nm.
This gives $4.00\times10^{-7}$ m to $7.00\times10^{-7}$ m.

ai_rubric.observable: States the approximate visible range as 400 to 700 nm.
Uses $1$ nm $=10^{-9}$ m to convert the endpoints.
Gives $4.00\times10^{-7}$ m to $7.00\times10^{-7}$ m or an exact equivalent.

hints: Place each value on a power-of-ten scale.
walkthrough: $2.3\times10^{-2}$ m lies between about $10^{-3}$ m and $10^{-1}$ m, so it is microwave.
$3.0\times10^{-6}$ m lies in the infrared range.
$5.5\times10^{-7}$ m is 550 nm, so it is visible.

hints: At fixed c, compare frequency by reversing the wavelength order.
walkthrough: The largest wavelength gives the lowest frequency.
Order the wavelengths from largest to smallest: $2.3\times10^{-2}$ m, $3.0\times10^{-6}$ m, $5.5\times10^{-7}$ m.
This is the required lowest-to-highest frequency order because c is constant.

ai_rubric.observable: Places the $2.3\times10^{-2}$ m wave first and the $3.0\times10^{-6}$ m wave second.
Explains that frequency increases as wavelength decreases because c is constant in free space.

hints: Rearrange c = f lambda for wavelength.
walkthrough: Use $\lambda=c/f$.
Substitute $(3.00\times10^8)/(3.75\times10^{14})$.
The wavelength is $8.00\times10^{-7}$ m. Multiplying it by the frequency returns $3.00\times10^8$ m s$^{-1}$.

hints: Divide the metre value by $10^{-9}$ m per nm.
walkthrough: $8.00\times10^{-7}$ m equals 800 nm.
The visible range ends at approximately 700 nm.
A wavelength just longer than this lies in the infrared region.

hints: At fixed c, doubling frequency halves wavelength.
walkthrough: Doubling frequency halves 800 nm to 400 nm.
This is $4.00\times10^{-7}$ m.
Four hundred nanometres is the approximate short-wavelength edge of visible light, next to ultraviolet, so state the boundary convention rather than claiming false precision.

ai_rubric.observable: States that the doubled-frequency wave has wavelength $4.00\times10^{-7}$ m or 400 nm.
Places 400 nm at the approximate visible-ultraviolet boundary and gives a boundary-aware classification.
